title: Answer openly
hookLine: think only thoughts you could say out loud if suddenly asked (Meditations 3.4)

cards: Penny for your thoughts. Someone says it across the table, and for a split second there's a small panic. The honest answer might be: I was replaying that argument and winning it this time.
Or comparing my life to my cousin's. Or wondering what those two are whispering about. So we say, oh, nothing.
Marcus turns that little moment into a test, not for what you say, but for what you think. Today: answer openly.

teach.h: DON'T SPEND LIFE ON OTHERS' DOINGS.
teach.b: Book three's fourth entry starts with a warning.
Don't waste what's left of your life thinking about other people, Marcus says, unless it's for some common good: what so-and-so is doing and why, what they're saying, what they're scheming.
All of that pulls you away from watching your own ruling part. Last week he warned against prying into other people's souls. Here it's how much of our own quiet thinking drifts to them.
Then the test. Get used to thinking only thoughts that, if someone suddenly asked what you're thinking right now, you could answer at once, openly: this, or that.
Then it would be plain, he says, that everything in you is simple and kind, fit for someone who lives among others.
No thought of pleasure or indulgence, no rivalry, no envy, no suspicion, nothing you'd blush to admit. It's a high bar. But notice his verb: get used to it.

teach.h: A SERVANT OF THE SPIRIT WITHIN.
teach.b: A person like that, he says, is like a priest and servant of the gods, at home with the divine within, untouched by pleasure, unhurt by pain, wrestling in the noblest contest, not overthrown by any passion.
Readers on different paths hear that differently; Marcus meant the spirit within he tended all through book two. The test itself fits anyone. Not a vow of perfect thoughts.
Just a question to ask before a thought settles in: could I say it?

how: Some people practicing Stoicism use Marcus's test during the day, asking whether their current thought is one they could say out loud without embarrassment.

o: confessing your private thoughts to someone every day
always saying exactly what you think, whatever it costs
keeping only thoughts you could say aloud if someone asked

p: don't spend your life on them

s: Marcus says never think about other people at all
not unless it's for some common good.
Marcus calls passing this test a habit to get used to
the test is about what you say, not what you think
it's about thoughts: could you say them openly if asked?

games.q: you're replaying a rival's mistake with some satisfaction, and someone asks what you're thinking. what does Meditations 3.4 point to?
o: notice you'd blush to say it, and let the thought go.
share it; it's honest, at least.
games.why: think only what you could say at once, openly, Marcus says: nothing of rivalry, envy or suspicion.

practice: Let your thoughts come and go, then imagine someone kind across from you asking gently: what are you thinking right now? If you could say it out loud, fine.
If not, don't scold yourself; just ask what the thought needs, to be let go or turned into something you could say.

wordCard.voice: Answer openly. Marcus: think only thoughts you could say out loud at once if someone suddenly asked, nothing you'd blush to admit. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: simple, single. Marcus wants every thought simple and kind enough to say aloud.

carryVoice: Your line: could I say it. A habit, built one thought at a time. That's day five hundred forty-one.
